traveler: San Brendan de Clonfert (Breanainn moccu Alti, Brendan the Navigator)
title: The Hide Boat and the Promised Land: Brendan of Kerry, the Navigatio, and the Island That Would Not Stay Off the Charts
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Fenit, Tralee Bay: a son born to Findlug and Cara
stops.date_confidence: Traditional. The year 484 comes from the Vita Sancti Brendani, a hagiography surviving in copies no earlier than the end of the twelfth century; no contemporary document attests Brendan's birth, and the month and day are unrecorded.
stops.campa: Findlug and Cara of the Alta race have a son near Tralee Bay, in the Ciarraige Luachra country of west Munster. The tradition gives the year as 484 and the place as the shore under low hills where the tide runs out a mile at slack water. He is called Mobhi first, then Broen-finn, the fair drop, and it is the second name that shortens and sticks. The bay below the settlement keeps him in local speech as the water of his first years, three hundred years before anyone writes the voyage down.
suggested_refs: The Vita Sancti Brendani birth narrative, Salamanca and Oxford recensions
sources: Vita Sancti Brendani (Salamanca and Oxford recensions)

stops.name: Tralee: baptized by Erc, fostered by Ita, schooled at Tuam
stops.date_confidence: Traditional, and internally contradictory. The pool carries both the statement that Brendan went to Jarlath's school at Tuam at age six, i.e. c. 490, and a dated entry placing the Tuam schooling at 500. Both readings are kept here; neither is documentary.
stops.campa: Bishop Erc of Slane baptizes the child at Tubrid near Ardfert. At five he is handed to Ita of Killeedy, who keeps him another five years and is remembered ever after as his foster mother and as the one voice whose rebuke he obeys. At six, by one account, he goes north to Bishop Jarlath's school at Tuam; another reckoning in the same record dates the Tuam years to 500, which would make him sixteen. Both numbers sit side by side. He returns to Erc for Scripture and is ordained priest at about twenty-six.
suggested_refs: The well at Tubrid near Ardfert, traditional baptismal site
Killeedy, Co. Limerick, the house of St Ita

stops.name: Ardfert: the cells founded in his own country
stops.date_confidence: Traditional. The pin is the ordination year, given as about age twenty-six. The Ardfert and Shanakeel foundations carry a date of 520 in the same hagiographic chronology, which places them after that chronology's own start for the voyage in 512; the sequence is unreconciled in the sources.
stops.campa: Erc ordains him priest, and Brendan begins founding: cells at Ardfert and at Shanakeel under the shoulder of the mountain, a base in his own country that his later fame at Clonfert never displaces. Kerry keeps him. The cathedral standing on the Ardfert site now is centuries younger than anything he raised, and the round tower and holy well that devotional accounts attach to him are not in the national monuments record for the place. What is here is a foundation the tradition dates and no document confirms.
suggested_refs: Ardfert Cathedral and its precinct, National Monuments Service record
sources: National Monuments Service Ireland, Ardfert Cathedral record

stops.name: Killeany, Inishmore: counsel from Enda before the sea
stops.date_confidence: Traditional. The Aran visit and the angelic redirection to the Shannon are hagiographic episodes; the 512 date belongs to the same schematic chronology that dates the voyage's start, and no annal records the visit.
stops.campa: He crosses to Enda's monastery on Aran, the hardest school in Ireland, to take counsel before the sea. Tradition holds that an angel meets him on the island and turns him east instead, toward the Shannon bank where Clonfert will rise, and that the same journey leaves a foundation of his own on the islands. Enda, Ciaran, Columba, Brendan: one generation fixes the map of Irish monasticism. Every Life of every one of them puts the others in the room at some point, and the genre requires that meeting more often than the record supports it.
suggested_refs: Betha Enda and the Aran monastic remains at Killeany

segments.name: The Mountain and the Hide Boat

stops.name: Kilmalkedar: the waypoint on Cosan na Naomh
stops.date_confidence: Site tradition only. The standing church fabric is seventh to twelfth century and the pilgrim route's association with Brendan is undated local tradition; the 512 pin is narrative placement, not evidence.
stops.campa: The church at Kilmalkedar stands on Cosan na Naomh, the Saint's Road, the pilgrim route that climbs from the Dingle shore to the summit of Brandon. An ogham stone and a stone sundial in the churchyard are older than the Romanesque building around them, which proves a Christian site here well before the surviving fabric and proves nothing about who founded it. Pilgrims walking to the mountain on the sixteenth of May still pass this gate. The road is called his; the stones are not signed.
suggested_refs: The ogham stone and stone sundial in the Kilmalkedar churchyard
sources: National Monuments Service Ireland, Kilmalkedar record

stops.name: Mount Brandon: three days of fasting above the open water
stops.date_confidence: Local tradition, undated. Kerry memory places the pre-voyage fast on the summit; the Navigatio names no Irish mountain at all, and the summit oratory Seipeilin Breanainn is not dated by any reachable source.
stops.campa: Cnoc Breanainn rises nine hundred and fifty-two metres over the Dingle peninsula, and from the summit the Atlantic runs west with nothing in it. Tradition sets Brendan here for three days of fasting and prayer before he goes down to the boat, at an oratory called Seipeilin Breanainn whose stones pilgrims still pass. The Navigatio names this mountain nowhere, and names no other in Ireland either. Kerry names it for him anyway, and the feast-day climb has never stopped.
suggested_refs: Seipeilin Breanainn, the summit oratory of Mount Brandon
The Cosan na Naomh pilgrim route
sources: local hagiographic tradition; pilgrim route records

stops.name: Brandon Creek: the first boat, and Ita's rebuke
stops.date_confidence: Traditional, and flatly contradicted between texts. The Vita has a failed hide-boat voyage corrected by Ita into a wooden ship with sixty disciples; the Navigatio has the hide boat succeed with fourteen. No date attaches to either.
stops.campa: The first attempt fails. Brendan builds a corach of hides, as the coast has always built them, and does not reach the promised land in it; he goes back to Ita at Killeedy, who fostered him, and she tells him the boat is the reason. He builds a wooden ship instead and sails again with sixty disciples. The Navigatio, older and far more widely copied, says the opposite: the hide boat is the right boat, greased with fat, and fourteen monks go out in it. The two accounts of the one voyage do not agree on the hull.
stops.quote: Thou wilt not gain the Land of Promise borne in the hides of dead beasts. Thou wilt find it with a ship made of boards.
stops.quote_source: Life of Brendan (Vita), quoted in J. P. Crichton-Stuart (Marquess of Bute), "Brendan's Fabulous Voyage" (1893), Project Gutenberg ebook #17343
suggested_refs: The Vita's hide-boat episode, against the Navigatio's chapter 4 boatbuilding
sources: Vita Sancti Brendani, in Crichton-Stuart, 'Brendan's Fabulous Voyage' (1893)

stops.name: Brandon Creek: fourteen men and forty days' provisions
stops.date_confidence: Traditional. Brandon Creek as the launching place is Kerry tradition, not text: the Navigatio gives boat construction in detail and no Irish harbour by name. The 512 date is the hagiographic chronology's, not an annal's.
stops.campa: Cuas an Bhodaigh is a slot in the cliff barely wider than a boat, shingle at the head of it and swell running straight in off the ocean. From here, tradition says, Brendan and fourteen companions push off with provisions for forty days, the hull wood-framed and skinned in tanned ox hide dressed with fat and stitched. In some manuscripts three latecomers beg their way aboard at the last moment, and Brendan tells them to their faces that two of the three will not be coming home.
suggested_refs: Brandon Creek (Cuas an Bhodaigh), the traditional launching inlet

stops.name: North of the Faroes: the fire that wakes Jasconius
stops.date_confidence: Legendary; the pin is a modern approximation on the notional northward track and has no textual basis. The Navigatio gives no bearing, no distance, and no landmark for this episode.
stops.campa: They find a bare rock with no beach and no grass, land on it, and light a fire to cook. The ground shifts under the pot and starts to travel. The brothers reach the boat, and Brendan, who has known since they landed, tells them what has been carrying them. The episode passes out of the Navigatio into the whole marvel literature of medieval Europe and onto the maps: the whale mistaken for an island, the fire that wakes it. Readers hunting a real sea behind the story put this one in the water off Iceland.
stops.quote: Where we have been was not an island but the first fish of all that swim in the ocean, and he seeketh ever to bring his tail unto his mouth, but he cannot, because of his length. Jasconius is his name.
stops.quote_source: Navigatio Sancti Brendani, quoted in J. P. Crichton-Stuart (Marquess of Bute), "Brendan's Fabulous Voyage" (1893), Project Gutenberg ebook #17343
suggested_refs: The whale-island motif in medieval bestiaries and on the Carta Marina

stops.name: Mykines: the Island of Sheep and the tree full of birds
stops.date_confidence: Legendary, and the identification is contested. The Faroes as model for the Island of Sheep is genuine scholarship; pinning either episode to Mykines specifically is not sourced, and Mykines is a seabird island whose Irish name means pig island.
stops.campa: The Navigatio brings them to an island bare of trees and crowded with white sheep the size of stags, where they keep Holy Thursday, and then to a tree filled with white birds, one of which comes down and speaks. Since the nineteenth century readers have proposed the Faroes as the model, an archipelago whose Norse name means sheep islands. Mykines, the westernmost of them, holds some hundred and twenty-five thousand pairs of puffins and no particular sheep, and its name is older Irish: muc-innis, pig island.
stops.quote: We are of that great ruin of the old enemy; but we have not fallen by sinning or consenting; but we have been predestinated by the goodness and mercy of God, for wherein we were created, hath our ruin come to pass, through his fall and the fall of his crew. But God the Almighty, Who is righteous and true, hath by His judgment sent us into this place. Pains we suffer not.
stops.quote_source: Navigatio Sancti Brendani, quoted in J. P. Crichton-Stuart (Marquess of Bute), "Brendan's Fabulous Voyage" (1893), Project Gutenberg ebook #17343
suggested_refs: Carl Selmer's critical edition of the Navigatio (1959), ch. 10-11

stops.name: Mykines: the bird counts out the seven years
stops.date_confidence: Legendary. The seven-year span is the Navigatio's own architecture stated in the text; it is a literary structure, not a chronology, and no year can be attached to any leg of it.
stops.campa: The bird that answers Brendan also counts for him. One year of the voyage is done and six remain; every Easter will be kept where this one was kept; at the end of the seventh he will find what he set out for. The prophecy is the book's structure spoken aloud in the middle of the book, and the voyage that follows obeys it exactly, returning each year to the same islands in the same order. It is a liturgical calendar wearing the clothes of a sea chart, and the reader is told so before the wonders begin.
stops.quote: As for thee, thou and thy brethren are a year upon the way, and yet there await you six. And where this day thou hast kept the Passover, there shall ye keep it every year, and afterwards shall thou find that which thou hast set in thine heart, even the land promised unto the Saints.
stops.quote_source: Navigatio Sancti Brendani, quoted in J. P. Crichton-Stuart (Marquess of Bute), "Brendan's Fabulous Voyage" (1893), Project Gutenberg ebook #17343
suggested_refs: The Navigatio's liturgical cycle: Maundy Thursday on the Island of Sheep, Easter on Jasconius

stops.name: The Isle of Ailbe: twenty-four monks who do not speak
stops.date_confidence: Legendary and unlocated. No source places this island anywhere; the coordinates here are a declared placeholder on the notional track, carry no evidentiary weight, and should not be read as an identification.
stops.campa: An island monastery of twenty-four monks under an abbot named Ailbe: silent for eighty years, fed by loaves that appear on the table with no baker, lit at the hours by a flame that arrives and departs without a hand. None of them has been ill and none has died. Brendan's crew keeps Christmas there and is not permitted to stay. The episode is the Irish ascetic ideal set down as a place, and it is the one island in the book that no commentator has ever tried to find on water.
suggested_refs: Navigatio ch. 12-13, the Ailbe community as monastic utopia

stops.name: Hekla: the island of smiths and the mountain on fire
stops.date_confidence: Legendary, with an interpretive identification laid over it. The volcanic reading is old and widely held; the Navigatio itself names no coast, and Hekla is a candidate among several rather than an attested location.
stops.campa: North of everything they pass an island of forges under a stink of smoke, and a blackened islander runs down to the shore and throws a lump of burning slag after the boat; the sea boils where it falls. Beyond it stands a mountain on fire. Brendan tells the crew where they are before he tells them anything else. Commentators from the medieval period onward read the passage as Iceland reported by somebody who had been there, with Hekla the usual candidate, and the text names no coast at all.
stops.quote: O ye soldiers of Christ, make you strong in faith not feigned, and in the armour of the spirit, for we are upon the coasts of hell. Watch, therefore, and play the man.
stops.quote_source: Navigatio Sancti Brendani, quoted in J. P. Crichton-Stuart (Marquess of Bute), "Brendan's Fabulous Voyage" (1893), Project Gutenberg ebook #17343
suggested_refs: Navigatio ch. 23-24 against the eruption history of Hekla

stops.name: Rockall: Judas on the rock, one night longer
stops.date_confidence: Legendary; the location is a commentator's guess with no textual basis. The Navigatio fixes nothing about the rock except that it is bare and alone, and Rockall is simply the loneliest outcrop later readers could name.
stops.campa: On a bare rock in open ocean a man sits in the spray, a cloth flapping on two iron prongs in front of him. It is Judas Iscariot, let out of hell on Sundays and feast days to cool himself here, the respite bought by a cloak and two towels he once gave away in life. Brendan asks for one more night for him and gets it, and the demons come at dawn to take him back down. No source fixes the rock. Commentators reach for the loneliest outcrops the Atlantic has, and Rockall is one of them.
suggested_refs: Navigatio ch. 25; Matthew Arnold's poem 'St. Brandan' on the same episode

stops.name: Paul the Hermit's rock: sixty years on an otter's charity
stops.date_confidence: Legendary and unlocated. The coordinates are a declared placeholder, not an identification; no source in the pool locates this rock, and its hermit is a type imported from Egyptian desert literature.
stops.campa: A rock with a spring on it holds a man ninety years old, clothed in nothing but his own white hair, who has lived here sixty years on water and on food an otter brings him out of the sea. He tells Brendan the voyage will end where it was aimed from the start. The figure is Egyptian, lifted whole from the desert fathers and set down on an Atlantic stone, and the Navigatio makes no secret of the borrowing. Nothing in the text locates the rock and nothing since has located it either.
suggested_refs: Navigatio ch. 26; the desert-father hermit type in Irish monastic literature

stops.name: The northern ice: a pillar of crystal in the open sea
stops.date_confidence: Legendary; the pin is a modern approximation of iceberg waters between Iceland and Greenland and rests on the interpretive reading, not on the text, which gives no position.
stops.campa: A column of clear crystal stands out of the sea, its head lost in cloud and its foot beyond any sounding they can take, and a mesh like a net hangs around it that takes them a whole day to row through. The water beside it is clear enough to show the base. Readers of the last two centuries take the passage for an iceberg carried home in somebody's memory, and it is the driest and most physical wonder in the book, described the way an instrument would describe it rather than the way a homilist would.
suggested_refs: Navigatio ch. 22, the crystal pillar and its mesh

stops.name: The Promised Land of the Saints: the river they may not cross
stops.date_confidence: Legendary. The coordinates here are not a location but a record of where later cartographers put the island, out in the Atlantic west of the Canaries; the Navigatio locates it only beyond a wall of fog.
stops.campa: Seven years out, the crew comes through a fog standing like a wall and lands in the country the whole voyage was aimed at: fruit ripe on every tree, light with no sun in it, stones of value lying loose on the ground, and a river across the middle they are forbidden to cross. A young man tells Brendan the land has been waiting since the world began and stays hidden until the Christians are persecuted. He takes fruit and stones for proof and turns for Ireland. Cartographers spend the next thousand years arguing about where he had been.
stops.quote: an holy land, polluted by no blood, open for the burial of no sinner, ... a land like Eden
stops.quote_source: Life of Brendan (Vita), quoted in J. P. Crichton-Stuart (Marquess of Bute), "Brendan's Fabulous Voyage" (1893), Project Gutenberg ebook #17343
suggested_refs: Navigatio ch. 28-29, the Terra Repromissionis Sanctorum

stops.name: Clonfert: the monastery on the east bank of the Shannon
stops.date_confidence: Contested across four values. One account gives c. 557, the corpus's own geography lens gives c. 559, the annals record the foundation at the order of an angel in 561, and the cathedral's account gives 563. The year is tradition, not an attested date; none of the four is adjudicated here.
stops.campa: On the east bank of the Shannon in Galway, Brendan founds the monastery that carries his name into every later calendar: Clonfert, a school said at its height to hold three thousand monks, one of the great houses of early Irish learning. The year is not settled. One account gives 557, another 559, the annals record the foundation at the order of an angel in 561, and the cathedral's own reckoning says 563. Four years for one event, and the founder is meant to be in his seventies through all of them.
suggested_refs: The Hiberno-Romanesque west doorway of Clonfert Cathedral, c. 1180

stops.name: Iona: Columba's island, and the synod that was not held here
stops.date_confidence: Doubtful as a location. Adomnan's Vita Columbae sets the Brendan and Columba episode at a synod at Teilte in Ireland, not on Iona, and the Iona house's own record does not mention Brendan; the date is placement within the generation, not an attested year.
stops.campa: Columba's community on Iona belongs to the same generation and the same impulse: an Irish monk puts an island between himself and his country and calls the exile peregrinatio. Adomnan's Life of Columba does bring Brendan on stage, but not here. He sets the meeting at a synod at Teilte in Ireland, where Columba stands excommunicated and Brendan crosses the floor to kiss him, saying he can see holy angels walking beside the man the synod has just condemned. Iona's own records do not mention Brendan at all.
suggested_refs: Adomnan, Vita Columbae, Book III, the synod at Teilte

stops.name: Annaghdown: the house for his sister Briga
stops.date_confidence: Doubted at the source. Francis Byrne questioned the plausibility of the grant to Brendan, and the earliest evidence for the site, from around 800, associates it with Ciaran rather than Brendan; the 560 date is traditional only.
stops.campa: At Annaghdown on the eastern shore of Lough Corrib, Brendan founds a monastery and beside it a convent for his sister Briga, who becomes its abbess. He is an old man by now and the foundations have run the length of the country, Kerry to Clare to Galway. The grant is doubted. Francis Byrne questioned whether it happened at all, and the earliest evidence for the site, from around 800, ties it to Ciaran and not to Brendan. What the tradition needs of Annaghdown is a sister and a house to die in, and it supplies both.
suggested_refs: The medieval remains at Annaghdown, Co. Galway

stops.name: Annaghdown: he tells Briga where she will rise
stops.date_confidence: Traditional. The Vita's deathbed sequence carries no dates of its own; the day here is set three days before the traditional feast, following the Vita's own count. The Vita also makes Brendan ninety-six, which cannot be squared with 484 to 577.
stops.campa: Visiting Briga, he tells her she will not be raised from this ground. She belongs to Tralee, and she is to go there, because the people of that country will find mercy through her. This place, he says, is a place of men and not of women. Then he tells her that God is calling him out of the prison of the body. The Vita has him in his ninety-sixth year while dating his birth to 484 and his death to 577, which makes ninety-three, and the text carries both numbers without pausing over either.
stops.quote: Not here shalt thou rise again, but in thine own land, that is in Tralee. Therefore, go thou thither, for that people will obtain the mercy of God by thy means. This is a place of men, not of women. Now is God calling me unto Himself out of the prison house of this body.
stops.quote_source: Vita Sancti Brendani, quoted in J. P. Crichton-Stuart (Marquess of Bute), "Brendan's Fabulous Voyage" (1893), Project Gutenberg ebook #17343
suggested_refs: The Vita's deathbed sequence at Annaghdown
sources: Vita Sancti Brendani, in Crichton-Stuart, 'Brendan's Fabulous Voyage' (1893)

stops.name: Annaghdown: the fear of the road, three days before the end
stops.date_confidence: The feast day, 16 May, is fixed and standard in the martyrologies. The year is not: the Annals of the Four Masters give 577 and the Annals of Ulster give 583, and the two are left unreconciled here.
stops.campa: Three days before the end he says what he is afraid of, and it is not the ocean. The man the whole legend is built on, who went west into unknown water for seven years and came back, says he fears travelling alone, and the dark road, and the face of the King, and the sentence of the Judge. Briga answers that they will all die at his death, since none of them could live in his absence. The Vita puts the day at the sixteenth of May. The Four Masters give the year 577 and the Annals of Ulster give 583.
stops.quote: I fear that I shall journey alone, that the way will be dark—I fear the unknown country, the presence of the King, the sentence of the Judge.
stops.quote_source: Vita Sancti Brendani, quoted in J. P. Crichton-Stuart (Marquess of Bute), "Brendan's Fabulous Voyage" (1893), Project Gutenberg ebook #17343
suggested_refs: The 16 May entry in the Irish martyrologies
sources: Vita Sancti Brendani, in Crichton-Stuart, 'Brendan's Fabulous Voyage' (1893)

stops.name: Clonfert: the body brought home in a farm cart
stops.date_confidence: The burial at Clonfert is the constant across all accounts; the concealment and the cart are a later legendary elaboration, and the date here follows the traditional 577 death year, which the Annals of Ulster contradict with 583.
stops.campa: His household knows what a famous corpse is worth. Rather than let Annaghdown keep him and grow a shrine over him, they conceal the death, wrap the body, and drive it home by night in a farm cart rather than on a bier, so that Clonfert alone will hold the relics. He is buried inside the monastery he founded. A grave slab in the cathedral grounds is shown to pilgrims into the modern era. The smuggling is a late elaboration; that Clonfert has the grave is the one thing every source agrees on.
stops.quote: Salute my friends on my behalf, and say unto them to beware of evil speaking, even when it is true, how much the more when it is false.
stops.quote_source: Vita Sancti Brendani, quoted in J. P. Crichton-Stuart (Marquess of Bute), "Brendan's Fabulous Voyage" (1893), Project Gutenberg ebook #17343
suggested_refs: The grave slab shown as Brendan's in the Clonfert Cathedral grounds
sources: Vita Sancti Brendani, in Crichton-Stuart, 'Brendan's Fabulous Voyage' (1893)
National Monuments Service Ireland, Clonfert Cathedral record

stops.name: Inishglora: an island house nobody's Life names
stops.date_confidence: Local tradition only, undated. No Life of Brendan names Inishglora; the association belongs to west-coast folklore, and the sixth-century date is a convention of that folklore rather than a finding.
stops.campa: Off the Mullet peninsula in Mayo, Inishglora holds an early monastic enclosure and a local tradition that puts it inside Brendan's circle of island houses. No Life of Brendan names the island. The same rock carries the end of the Children of Lir, where the swans come ashore, are baptized, and die as ancient people, so Inishglora is already doing legendary work before Brendan is attached to it. The west coast has a hundred of these, and the folklore distributes founders across them generously.
suggested_refs: The monastic enclosure on Inishglora, National Monuments Service record
sources: National Monuments Service Ireland, Inishglora record

stops.name: Skellig Michael: what the discipline actually looked like
stops.date_confidence: The monastic settlement is dated broadly to the sixth to eighth centuries and no source places Brendan on the rock; the date is a mid-point of that range, and the stop is milieu rather than itinerary.
stops.campa: Twelve kilometres off the Kerry coast, six hundred steps of dry stone climb to a shelf of beehive cells and two oratories built on a rock with no soil and no shelter. Nobody claims Brendan here. The rock supplies the physical fact the Navigatio takes for granted: men chose this over arable land, deliberately, and called the choosing prayer. The islands of silent monks and hair-clothed hermits in the Navigatio are not made out of nothing. There is one of them in the water off his own county.
suggested_refs: The Skellig Michael monastic settlement and its two oratories
sources: National Monuments Service Ireland, Skellig Michael record

stops.name: Gallarus: a boat turned over in stone
stops.date_confidence: The construction date is openly disputed, sixth to ninth century in the standard range. Peter Harbison proposed a twelfth-century date in 1970 and abandoned it in 1994-95 for a pilgrim-shelter reading; the 800 pin is the mid-range, not a finding.
stops.campa: A dry-stone chapel near the foot of Mount Brandon, corbelled without mortar, still watertight, shaped so nearly like an upturned boat that the comparison has become standard. Its date is disputed. Peter Harbison proposed the twelfth century in 1970 and abandoned that reading in the mid-1990s in favour of a pilgrim shelter. It stands on the road to Brandon and gets folded into every modern retelling of the voyage. No source calls Brendan its builder, and nothing in the stone requires him.
suggested_refs: Peter Harbison's two readings of Gallarus Oratory, 1970 and 1994-95
sources: National Monuments Service Ireland, Gallarus Oratory record

segments.name: The Book That Outsailed the Man

stops.name: Clonfert: the Navigatio written, two centuries late
stops.date_confidence: Scholarly consensus places composition in the second half of the eighth century; no year, author, or house is known, and the attribution of the writing to Clonfert specifically is an assumption of place, not a finding.
stops.campa: Two centuries after the abbot dies, someone in an Irish monastery writes the Navigatio Sancti Brendani Abbatis: not a life of a saint but a voyage, seven years of islands in Latin prose, organised by the liturgical year. Scholars place the composition in the second half of the eighth century, which puts it before the Vita rather than after it. The book that made Brendan famous is therefore older than the biography of him, and the biography contradicts it about the boat that carried him.
suggested_refs: Carl Selmer, Navigatio Sancti Brendani Abbatis, critical edition (1959)

stops.name: Paris: a hundred manuscripts and a queen's translation
stops.date_confidence: The oldest surviving witness is dated to about 900 and is Continental; the pin is the corpus's canonical Paris coordinate standing for Continental transmission generally, not the location of any particular manuscript or scriptorium.
stops.campa: The oldest surviving copy dates to about 900 and is Continental, not Irish. Over a hundred manuscripts of the Navigatio survive from across medieval Europe, and the translations run past counting. Benedeit turns it into Anglo-Norman verse around 1121 for Adeliza of Louvain, queen to Henry I of England, and later readers call that poem an ancestor of Old French romance. A Middle Dutch version, De Reis van Sinte Brandaen, comes out of a lost German text crossed with Gaelic material carried over from Ireland.
suggested_refs: Benedeit's Anglo-Norman Voyage of St Brendan, dedicated to Adeliza of Louvain
De Reis van Sinte Brandaen, Middle Dutch

stops.name: Papa Westray: the priests the Norse say they found
stops.date_confidence: Place-name evidence, not documentary. The papar names are Norse reports of predecessors and cannot be dated closely; nothing connects Brendan personally to Orkney, and the 800 pin marks the settlement horizon.
stops.campa: The name is Old Norse: papar, priests. Orkney and Shetland are scattered with these names, and they record what the Norse settlers said they found when they arrived, which is Irish clerics already living on the islands. No source puts Brendan on Papa Westray or on any of the others. What the place-names establish is that the current the legend rides on was real. Irish monks did go out into this ocean, island by island, north and west, before anyone wrote the Navigatio down.
suggested_refs: W. P. L. Thomson, The New History of Orkney, on the papar place-names
sources: W. P. L. Thomson, The New History of Orkney

stops.name: Papey: the documents say monks, the ground says otherwise
stops.date_confidence: Dicuil's Liber de Mensura Orbis Terrae is firmly dated to 825 and the Landnamabok reference is genuine; the archaeology on Papey found Norse settlement and no monastic trace, so the identification of the island with actual papar occupation is documentary only.
stops.campa: Papey, priests' island, off the Icelandic east coast, is named the same way and for the same reason. Dicuil, writing in 825, records Irish clerics who had sailed to Thule and seen a summer night too bright to hide a louse in a shirt, which is a report from somebody who was there. The Landnamabok says the Norse found papar in Iceland and that they went away. Then the archaeology: survey on Papey turned up Norse settlement and no monastic trace at all. The documents and the ground do not agree.
suggested_refs: Dicuil, Liber de Mensura Orbis Terrae (825), on Irish clerics at Thule
sources: Dicuil, Liber de Mensura Orbis Terrae (825)

stops.name: Kirkjubaer on the Sida: the church-name before the church
stops.date_confidence: The papar tradition for Kirkjubaer is attested in the Landnamabok; the farm's later role in Njal's saga is saga narrative and no year attaches to the transition from Irish to Norse occupation.
stops.campa: At Kirkjubaer on the Sida the tradition says the papar held the ground before the Norse took it, and the name means church-farm from before there was a Norse church to name it after. The corpus reaches this place through the saga of Burnt Njal, where it is simply a farm inside a feud and nobody stops to explain the name. Iceland converts by a vote at the Althing around the year 1000, four centuries after Brendan dies, and the Irish clerics who were there first get one line in the record and no names.
suggested_refs: The Landnamabok notice of the papar at Kirkjubaer on the Sida

stops.name: Brattahlid: the fjord Leif Erikson sails from, or does not
stops.date_confidence: The estate is firmly identified as Erik the Red's, but the departure point for the Vinland voyage is contested: Graenlendinga saga sails Leif from Greenland, Eiriks saga rauda has him leaving Norway and driven off course. The contradiction is not resolved here.
stops.campa: Erik the Red's estate at the head of Eiriksfjord in Greenland is where Leif Erikson is raised and where he keeps coming back to. The sagas disagree about where he sailed from for Vinland: one has him leaving this fjord, the other has him blown off a course out of Norway. Two Atlantic launches five centuries apart, one from a slot in a Kerry cliff and one from this water, and only one of them has a farm that can be dug. The same saga carries a report of a country of people dressed in white carrying poles, which antiquarians later called Greater Ireland.
stops.quote: there was a land on the other side over against their land, and the people there were dressed in white garments, uttered loud cries, bare long poles, and wore fringes. This was supposed to be Hvitramannaland (whiteman's land).
stops.quote_source: Eiriks saga rauda (Saga of Erik the Red), English translation, sagadb.org
suggested_refs: Thjodhild's church at Brattahlid (Qassiarsuk), excavated 1961
The Hvitramannaland / Greater Ireland notice in Eiriks saga rauda

stops.name: L'Anse aux Meadows: the crossing that left iron behind
stops.date_confidence: Attested archaeologically, and dated far more precisely than any Brendan claim: wood cut with metal tools at the site is dated to the year 1021 by a cosmic-ray event recorded in the tree rings.
stops.campa: Eight sod buildings, a smithy, iron rivets, a spindle whorl, and wood cut with metal tools in the year 1021, dated to the year by a solar storm written into the tree rings. This is the only confirmed pre-Columbian European site in North America and it belongs to Leif Erikson's people. The corpus sets it beside Brendan deliberately. One landfall stands on excavated timber and iron; the other stands on a manuscript copied a hundred times over, and it was the manuscript that travelled further.
stops.quote: Leif was tossed about a long time out at sea, and lighted upon lands of which before he had no expectation. There were fields of wild wheat, and the vine-tree in full growth.
stops.quote_source: Eiriks saga rauda (Saga of Erik the Red), English translation, sagadb.org
suggested_refs: Parks Canada, L'Anse aux Meadows National Historic Site excavation reports
sources: Parks Canada, L'Anse aux Meadows archaeological reports

stops.name: Hy-Brasil: the other island west of Ireland
stops.date_confidence: Attested cartographically from the Dulcert portolan of 1325 onward; the coordinates are the chart position, not a place, and the island does not exist.
stops.campa: From the fourteenth century, portolan charts mark a round island west of Ireland called Hy-Brasil, cut across the middle by a strait, and cartographers keep redrawing it into the nineteenth. It is not Brendan's island; it is the neighbour. The two phantoms run alongside each other on the same sheets for five hundred years, sometimes drawn on the one chart, and both are erased in the end by the same slow accumulation of ships that sailed there and found water.
suggested_refs: Angelino Dulcert's portolan chart of 1325 and its successors

stops.name: Iceland: Columbus hears the old men talk of lands further west
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the corpus's Columbus file: the February 1477 voyage past Galway to Thule and the old men's tales of western lands. That Brendan lore specifically reached him by that channel is inference, not record.
stops.campa: Columbus sails past Galway and north to Iceland in February 1477, a hundred leagues beyond Thule by his own account, and hears the old men there tell of lands further west. Greenland is a fact in Iceland by then and Vinland is a story that has been told for four centuries. Whatever reached him at that latitude reached him through the channel that also carried the papar and the western islands: monks, sagas, and sailors' report in one mouth, and no way now to separate the three of them out.
suggested_refs: The 1477 Thule passage in Columbus's own reported account

stops.name: Lisbon: Antilia drawn on a chart meant to be steered by
stops.date_confidence: The Toscanelli chart and its Antilia are attested in the corpus's Columbus file. The claim that Columbus knew the Navigatio's account of Atlantic winds comes from Paul Chapman and is not corroborated by Columbus's own writings in any source reachable here.
stops.campa: In Lisbon Columbus works from a copy of Toscanelli's chart, which sets Antilia, the island of the Seven Cities, in the middle of the ocean as a waystation on the road to Asia. Antilia is not St Brendan's Isle, but it is the same species of island: a place drawn onto a working navigational document by men who meant to steer by it. Some accounts hold that Columbus also knew the Navigatio's report of favourable winds west and north-about home. His own writings, in what is reachable, do not say so.
suggested_refs: The Toscanelli chart of 1474 and its Antilia, as carried by Columbus
sources: Paul Chapman thesis, as reported in Wikipedia, 'Brendan of Clonfert'

stops.name: Nuremberg: St Brendan's Island painted onto the Erdapfel
stops.date_confidence: The Erdapfel is firmly dated to 1492. The earlier map claims conflict: the Ebstorf map is placed between 1234 and 1240 by some and as late as 1300 by others, while Hereford is described as the earliest known map to show the island. Both cannot be first, and this file does not choose.
stops.campa: Martin Behaim finishes the Erdapfel at Nuremberg in 1492, the oldest terrestrial globe that survives, and St Brendan's Island is on it, out in the Atlantic west of the Canaries. Columbus is at sea while the paint dries. The island had reached the great wall maps long before: the Ebstorf map, made somewhere between 1234 and 1240 and burned in the bombing of Hanover in 1943, and the Hereford Mappa Mundi of about 1300, which Hereford calls the earliest known map to show it. Both claims cannot stand.
suggested_refs: The Erdapfel at the Germanisches Nationalmuseum, Nuremberg
The 1891 photographs of the destroyed Ebstorf map

stops.name: Las Palmas: Gran Canaria sends a ship to find it
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the Spanish record of San Borondon expeditions, which lists 1526 under Hernando de Troya and Francisco Alvarez. English-language accounts giving 1566, 1719 and 1759 are unsupported by that record and are not followed here.
stops.campa: Gran Canaria sends out a search. In 1526 Hernando de Troya and Francisco Alvarez sail west to find the island the Canaries can see and cannot reach, and they come back with nothing. It is not the first attempt, Fernando de Viseu having tried in the previous century, and it is nowhere near the last. Colonial administration in the archipelago treats San Borondon as a matter for expeditions and notarised testimony, which is to say as a real place that keeps failing to be where it was reported to be.
suggested_refs: The Canary Islands colonial records of the San Borondon expeditions

stops.name: La Palma: the eighth island, seen and not reached
stops.date_confidence: The 1721 Gaspar Dominguez voyage is recorded as the last official expedition. Sightings continue after it and the island stays on charts into the eighteenth century; the date marks the end of the official searches, not of the belief.
stops.campa: From La Palma, in certain weather, people see an eighth island in the west, wooded and mountainous, standing for an hour and then gone. They call it San Borondon. Expeditions go out in 1570 under Hernan Perez de Grado, in 1604 under Gaspar Perez de Acosta and Fray Lorenzo de Pinedo, and last in 1721 under Gaspar Dominguez, who finds open water. The sightings do not stop when the expeditions stop. The island holds its place on charts into the eighteenth century, two hundred and fifty years after Columbus.
suggested_refs: The 1721 Gaspar Dominguez expedition, last official search for San Borondon

stops.name: Brandon Creek: a leather boat put in the water again
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Tim Severin departed Brandon Creek in May 1976, wintered in Iceland, and completed the crossing the following summer; the day of departure is not given in the sources consulted here.
stops.campa: In May 1976 Tim Severin puts a boat into the water at Brandon Creek built from the Navigatio's own description: ash frame, ox hides tanned in oak bark, dressed with wool fat, stitched with leather thread. He calls it Brendan. The route runs by the Hebrides, the Faroes, and Iceland, wintering once on the way, which is the route the papar place-names would predict and the route onto which the Navigatio's islands are usually mapped. He is testing a hull, and he says so.
suggested_refs: Tim Severin, The Brendan Voyage (1978)

stops.name: Peckford Island: the hide boat comes ashore in Newfoundland
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day: landfall on Peckford Island in the Wadham group, 26 June 1977, followed by a tow into Musgrave Harbour by the Canadian Coast Guard.
stops.campa: On 26 June 1977 the leather boat comes ashore on Peckford Island in the Wadham group off Newfoundland, and the Canadian Coast Guard tows it in to Musgrave Harbour. A hide currach of sixth-century design can cross the North Atlantic; that is a fact now and it was not one before. It makes Brendan the discoverer of nothing. It moves the legend from impossible to unproven, a shorter distance than the enthusiasts want and a longer one than the sceptics had been allowing. Shaun Davey sets the voyage to orchestra in 1980.
suggested_refs: Shaun Davey, The Brendan Voyage, orchestral suite (1980)
